paragraphs: Slow Feature Analysis learns from the observation that meaningful properties can change more slowly than the signals used to perceive them. For time series, this provides a way to extract latent features by emphasizing temporal persistence. Previous results on naturalistic stimuli also connect SFA to properties of cells in the visual cortex and hippocampus, motivating its study as a possible principle of brain computation.

The paper addresses the gap between that computational principle and a plausible neural implementation. It derives an algorithm called Bio-SFA directly from an SFA objective. Biological plausibility has a specific meaning here: the algorithm processes observations online and can be implemented by a neural network whose synapses use local update rules.

The authors validate Bio-SFA on naturalistic stimuli. The contribution is therefore both an algorithm for learning slow features and an implementation that meets these stated biological constraints. This makes SFA more useful for investigating how temporal regularities could support neural learning, without establishing that the brain actually implements Bio-SFA.
neurips-2020-a-biologically-plausible-ne.tldr: Bio-SFA turns slow feature learning into an online neural algorithm with local synaptic updates and validates it on naturalistic stimuli.

paragraphs: A classifier used in sensitive applications may need to balance predictive accuracy with constraints on how its outputs relate to sensitive attributes. This paper studies that problem for binary classification, focusing on demographic parity and equalized odds. These are two particular definitions of group fairness, so the optimization target is a specified statistical relationship rather than fairness in every possible sense.

The method uses kernel density estimation to quantify the relevant fairness measures. Its key computational property is that these quantities are differentiable with respect to the classifier's parameters. That connects fairness constraints to gradient descent, allowing the training procedure to adjust predictions while accounting for the chosen fairness requirement.

Experiments on synthetic and real benchmark datasets report better accuracy–fairness tradeoffs than prior fair classifiers under both definitions. The stated result concerns the balance achieved between these objectives in the experiments. The broader contribution is a way to make group fairness measures directly usable within gradient-based classifier optimization.
neurips-2020-a-fair-classifier-using-ker.tldr: Kernel density estimation makes two group fairness measures differentiable, enabling classifier training with improved empirical accuracy–fairness tradeoffs.

paragraphs: A discrete probability distribution assigns weights to a collection of points, called atoms. Sometimes the quantities that matter are only the averages of a specified set of functions over those points. The paper considers how to shrink the distribution while preserving all of those selected averages exactly.

For a distribution on N atoms and n real-valued functions, a replacement distribution exists on at most n+1 of the original atoms with the same function averages. The task is to compute such a replacement. The authors give a geometric description of weighted centers using negative cones, then build a randomized algorithm called greedy geometric sampling around that description.

The authors study the algorithm's properties and benchmark it on synthetic and real data. They report particular benefits when the original number of atoms is much larger than the number of functions. The compression preserves the specified averages; it does not claim to preserve every property of the original distribution. Its value is reducing the representation needed for those selected quantities.
neurips-2020-a-randomized-algorithm-to-r.tldr: A randomized geometric algorithm compresses a discrete distribution while exactly preserving the averages of a specified set of functions.

paragraphs: Comparing two policies becomes difficult when each policy changes conditions that affect subsequent observations. In settings such as ridesharing or inventory management, this temporal interference can bias standard experiments. The paper frames the comparison as estimating the difference in long-run rewards between two unknown Markov chains, each representing a policy.

The analysis assumes that each chain's steady-state reward is estimated using nonparametric maximum likelihood. The authors seek experimental designs that become unbiased asymptotically and achieve asymptotically minimum variance. Although the associated minimum-variance decision problem is generally difficult, they use martingale analysis and Poisson's equation for Markov chains to characterize efficient designs through a compact convex optimization problem.

This characterization leads to an online experimental design that adaptively samples the two chains. The result links how an experiment allocates observations to the quality of its eventual policy comparison. Its consistency and efficiency are asymptotic statements under the stated estimation framework, rather than promises that temporal interference disappears immediately in a short experiment.
neurips-2020-adaptive-experimental-desig.tldr: The paper derives an adaptive policy experiment with asymptotic consistency and efficiency despite temporal interference.

paragraphs: Adversarial training exposes a neural network to deliberately perturbed inputs to address its sensitivity to those changes. Operator norm regularization approaches sensitivity through a mathematical measure of amplification. This paper establishes a theoretical connection between these approaches, providing a way to interpret a particular adversarial training procedure as a regularization method.

The equivalence has specific conditions. Perturbations are constrained by an lp norm and generated through projected gradient ascent, while the loss measures an lq norm difference between the logits for clean and perturbed inputs. Under this formulation, the authors prove equivalence to data-dependent (p, q) operator norm regularization. The choices of input and output norms are therefore part of the claim.

The connection supports the argument that adversarial sensitivity is tied to a network's spectral properties. Extensive experiments on contemporary network architectures support the theoretical findings. The result also suggests possible routes toward new defenses, while the stated equivalence concerns the specified training setup rather than every procedure described as adversarial training.
neurips-2020-adversarial-training-is-a-f.tldr: A specified norm-based adversarial training procedure is theoretically equivalent to data-dependent operator norm regularization.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovery of a rank-one signal matrix hidden inside additive Gaussian noise. The signal is constructed from a sparse vector whose nonzero entries grow more slowly in number than its total dimension. The analysis follows an asymptotic regime in which dimension grows and the signal-to-noise ratio also increases at an appropriate rate.

The authors derive explicit low-dimensional variational formulas for the mutual information between the signal and the observed matrix. They also analyze approximate message passing, an algorithm for estimating the hidden signal. For Bernoulli and Bernoulli-Rademacher vectors under suitable sparsity and signal scaling, both optimal and algorithmic mean-square errors exhibit abrupt transitions from their maximum values to zero.

The thresholds for these transitions are determined exactly in the asymptotic regime. The gap between statistically possible recovery and recovery by approximate message passing diverges there. This shows a growing separation between available information and what this algorithm can exploit, establishing difficulty for approximate message passing without making the same claim about every possible algorithm.
neurips-2020-all-or-nothing-statistical-.tldr: Under specified sparse asymptotic conditions, signal recovery has sharp thresholds and a diverging gap between optimal estimation and approximate message passing.

paragraphs: Probabilistic deep generative networks connect hidden variables to observed outputs, but training requires reasoning about distributions that can be difficult to calculate. Variational autoencoders address this difficulty using approximate inference and sampling. This paper investigates whether the mathematical structure of the generator can instead provide analytical access to the relevant distributions.

The authors exploit the continuous piecewise affine structure of modern generative networks: the mapping consists of affine pieces joined continuously. From this structure, they derive posterior and marginal distributions, together with the marginal distribution's first two moments. These results support an analytical expectation-maximization algorithm that learns the generative network without gradient-based training.

In the reported experiments, expectation-maximization training achieves greater likelihood than VAE training. That is empirical evidence for the proposed learning approach, rather than a universal ranking of the methods. The analytical framework also offers a basis for designing better variational approximations and for applying statistical tools to model comparison, anomaly detection, and missing-data imputation; these are presented as avenues opened by the work.
neurips-2020-analytical-probability-dist.tldr: The paper uses piecewise affine network structure to derive analytical distributions and a gradient-free expectation-maximization training method.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference can become expensive when it repeatedly uses a large dataset. A coreset reduces this burden by replacing the data with a small weighted subset. The paper identifies two difficulties with that strategy: high-dimensional posterior approximation can degrade, and retaining original observations creates an obstacle to preserving individual privacy.

The authors prove that there are situations where even the optimal coreset's Kullback-Leibler divergence from the full posterior grows with data dimension. They propose Bayesian pseudocoresets, which use a small weighted collection of synthetic observations. A variational optimization method chooses both the synthetic points and their weights, allowing the summary to move beyond selecting existing records.

Synthetic pseudodata enable high-dimensional summarization and differentially private summaries within the proposed approach. Experiments on real and synthetic high-dimensional data show substantial reductions in posterior approximation error compared with traditional coresets. They also show privacy without a significant loss in approximation quality in the tested settings. The contribution is a more flexible representation of the information needed for Bayesian inference.
neurips-2020-bayesian-pseudocoresets-b7d.tldr: Bayesian pseudocoresets optimize small weighted synthetic datasets to improve posterior approximation and enable differentially private summarization.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object becomes difficult when its appearance changes with its state or use. A tomato, for example, can look very different after slicing or cooking. Surrounding objects and activities provide clues about these changes, but manually labeling the open-ended combinations of objects, states, and contexts would require extensive annotation.

COBE learns contextualized object representations from instructional videos and their automatically transcribed narration. The visual detector is trained to predict a contextualized word embedding associated with the object and narration. Language supplies semantic relationships and compositional structure, giving the visual representation a way to organize related concepts beyond a fixed object name.

Experiments show that the detector predicts varied contextual information and works effectively in few-shot and zero-shot learning settings. These findings support using narration to learn richer object representations with less reliance on manually labeled examples for this task. The central contribution is connecting visual detection to language-derived context, so that an object's representation can reflect how it appears and is being used.
neurips-2020-cobe-contextualized-object-.tldr: COBE uses automatically transcribed instructional videos to learn object representations that capture visual states and context.

paragraphs: A coreset is a small summary of a dataset intended to retain the information needed for model training. Such summaries are useful when observations arrive continuously and resources prevent retaining or processing everything. The paper addresses a restriction of existing coreset constructions, which the abstract describes as being limited to relatively simple models such as k-means and logistic regression.

The proposed construction uses cardinality-constrained bilevel optimization. The cardinality constraint limits the size of the summary, while the two-level formulation connects summary construction with the model-training problem it is meant to support. This makes the choice of retained information part of an optimization framework directed toward training usefulness.

The authors show that their framework can efficiently construct coresets for deep neural networks and report empirical benefits in continual learning and streaming. The significance is extending compact training summaries to a more expressive class of models. The stated evidence supports their usefulness in these settings without asserting that every small summary exactly reproduces full-data training.
neurips-2020-coresets-via-bilevel-optimi.tldr: A size-constrained bilevel optimization framework constructs deep-network coresets with empirical benefits for continual learning and streaming.

paragraphs: A regression network predicts a continuous value, but its usefulness can also depend on knowing how uncertain that prediction is. This paper trains a non-Bayesian neural network to predict both the target and supporting evidence. The aim is to learn aleatoric uncertainty associated with the data and epistemic uncertainty associated with the model's knowledge.

The method places evidential priors over a Gaussian likelihood and makes the network infer the parameters of the evidential distribution. Additional training priors regularize predictions when the claimed evidence does not align with the correct output. In this way, the amount of support assigned to a prediction becomes something the training objective explicitly addresses.

Inference does not require sampling, and training does not require out-of-distribution examples. These properties support efficient uncertainty estimation. The authors demonstrate calibrated uncertainty on several benchmarks, application to complex computer vision tasks, and robustness on adversarial and out-of-distribution test samples. Those findings establish empirical behavior in the evaluated settings rather than a general safety guarantee.
neurips-2020-deep-evidential-regression-.tldr: Deep evidential regression learns continuous predictions and uncertainty evidence without inference-time sampling or out-of-distribution training examples.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust federated learning optimizes against a mixture of local losses through a minimax problem. Reducing communication complicates that objective: the global parameter controlling the mixture can only be updated intermittently. Local learning therefore has to proceed while information needed for the mixture update accumulates between communication rounds.

The proposed Distributionally Robust Federated Averaging algorithm combines periodic averaging and adaptive sampling with a snapshotting scheme. That scheme approximates accumulated historical gradients for the mixture parameter. The authors analyze convergence in convex-linear and nonconvex-linear settings, connecting reduced communication to guarantees for the distributed minimax objective.

They also introduce DRFA-Prox for objectives that regularize the mixture parameter and establish convergence rates for it. An alternative regularized method is analyzed under stronger curvature conditions, including a stated PL condition in one nonconvex setting. Federated learning experiments corroborate the theory. The contribution is an approach to communication-efficient robust federated optimization with guarantees tailored to these different mathematical settings.
neurips-2020-distributionally-robust-fed.tldr: DRFA uses gradient snapshots and periodic averaging to support distributionally robust federated learning with reduced communication and convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Clustering divides data into groups, but the computational burden can become substantial when there are many observations or many desired clusters. This paper revisits a framework that connects k-means with ratio-cut, bringing two established clustering viewpoints into a shared formulation. The authors use that connection to develop a new efficient clustering algorithm.

The stated time and memory complexities both grow linearly with the number of samples. More unusually, these complexities are independent of the number of clusters being constructed. These properties matter because increasing the dataset size or requesting more groups can otherwise make clustering difficult to scale to large practical problems.

The authors evaluate the method on 12 real-world benchmark datasets and eight facial datasets, reporting advantages over leading clustering algorithms. They specifically report speedups exceeding 15 times over k-means on a synthetic dataset with one million samples and seven times on CelebA with 200,000 samples. These are results for the named comparisons, supporting the algorithm's practical scaling benefits alongside its complexity claims.
neurips-2020-efficient-clustering-based-.tldr: A unified view of k-means and ratio-cut yields clustering with linear time and memory complexity independent of the number of clusters.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering organizes observations into a tree of nested groups. Dasgupta's objective assigns a global cost to such a tree, but optimizing over discrete tree structures is challenging. HypHC creates a continuous version of this problem by representing the tree's leaves as points in hyperbolic space and decoding those points back into a clustering tree.

The method develops a continuous counterpart of the lowest common ancestor, the point where two branches meet in a tree. This supplies the bridge between the discrete objective and its continuous relaxation. The authors prove that decoding a global minimizer of the relaxation gives a tree within a factor of 1+epsilon of optimal; making epsilon smaller affects optimization difficulty.

The guarantee specifically concerns a global minimizer. Separately, experiments show that approximate solutions obtained with gradient descent outperform agglomerative heuristics and other gradient-based methods on the evaluated benchmarks. An end-to-end classification application demonstrates flexibility. Together, the results connect a principled tree objective with continuous optimization while distinguishing the theoretical optimum from practical solutions.
neurips-2020-from-trees-to-continuous-em.tldr: HypHC optimizes hierarchical clustering through hyperbolic embeddings, with a near-optimal decoding guarantee for the relaxation's global minimizer.

paragraphs: Observed measurements may be effects of hidden causal variables rather than the variables whose relationships we want to discover. This paper studies linear, non-Gaussian latent variable models in which hidden confounders can themselves be causally related. Its goal is to locate those latent variables and recover their causal structure, including directions.

The proposed Generalized Independent Noise condition examines two vectors of observed variables. It holds when a linear combination of one vector is statistically independent of the other, with the combination characterized using their cross-covariance. Roughly, the graphical interpretation connects this independence to earlier latent common causes separating the two observed groups.

The familiar independence between causes and regression errors in the absence of confounding appears as a special case. The authors use the generalized condition to develop a recursive learning algorithm and show its effectiveness on synthetic and real data. The contribution extends independence-based causal reasoning to related hidden causes within the stated linear, non-Gaussian model class.
neurips-2020-generalized-independent-noi.tldr: A generalized noise-independence condition supports discovery of hidden variables and causal directions in linear, non-Gaussian latent models.

paragraphs: Feature-sparse principal component analysis combines feature selection with dimensionality reduction. It seeks a principal subspace while restricting which original features are used. The paper addresses the difficulty of optimizing this combined objective: the general problem is NP-hard, and the existing methods described in the abstract rely on distributional assumptions and lack global convergence guarantees.

The authors separate a tractable special case from the general setting. For low-rank covariance, their first algorithm can solve the problem globally. For general covariance, a second algorithm iteratively builds a carefully designed proxy problem. The global solution claim for low-rank covariance therefore does not automatically extend to arbitrary covariance matrices.

The analysis supplies data-dependent approximation bounds and convergence guarantees. It also provides particular approximation bounds when the covariance spectrum follows exponential or Zipf distributions. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show promising performance and efficiency relative to existing methods. The work contributes both algorithms and a more explicit account of how attainable solution quality depends on the covariance structure.
neurips-2020-learning-feature-sparse-pri.tldr: New feature-sparse PCA algorithms provide a global solution for low-rank covariance and approximation guarantees for more general cases.

paragraphs: Pretraining can help a prediction model by first teaching it related tasks, but choosing those tasks becomes difficult when many candidates have complicated relationships to the final objective. This paper develops an automatic selection method intended to find auxiliary tasks that produce a representation useful for a particular target task.

The method places auxiliary task selection inside a nested-loop meta-learning procedure. Its clinical application draws on electronic medical records, using many self-supervised forecasting tasks about patient trajectories as potential sources of pretraining. The selection process connects the choice of forecast tasks to their usefulness for clinical outcome prediction.

On a real clinical dataset, the approach outperforms direct supervised learning, naive pretraining, and multitask learning, especially when the primary task has few examples. Ablation analyses also indicate that the learned selection rules are interpretable and can generalize to unseen target tasks with new data. These results support learning which auxiliary tasks to use as an important part of representation learning.
neurips-2020-learning-to-select-best-for.tldr: Automatic selection of forecasting tasks improves clinical outcome prediction in experiments, particularly when target-task data are scarce.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a moving, deformable object from video requires more than producing a plausible 3D shape in each frame. The shapes should also remain consistent representations of the same object over time. This paper treats that requirement as an online adaptation problem, using the incoming test video itself to refine a reconstruction model.

The method first learns a category-specific model from single-view images belonging to the same category. That model jointly predicts shape, texture, and camera pose. During inference, self-supervised regularization adapts it over time so that reconstructed meshes share a texture map, a base shape, and parts. These shared elements connect the framewise reconstructions.

The video adaptation does not require per-frame annotations of 3D meshes, 2D keypoints, or camera pose. The authors demonstrate temporally consistent and reliable reconstructions for non-rigid objects, including animals filmed in the wild. The contribution is using an object's continuity through a video as supervision for adaptation, while starting from a learned model of its category.
neurips-2020-online-adaptation-for-consi.tldr: A category-specific reconstruction model adapts to test videos using temporal consistency to produce coherent 3D meshes of deformable objects.

paragraphs: In online learning with dynamics, a chosen policy affects costs within a world that has a changing state. This paper allows both state evolution and costs to vary over time, potentially adversarially. It studies policy regret, where evaluating decisions must account for the interaction between policies and the environment's evolving state.

The authors derive non-constructive upper bounds on the minimax rate and sufficient conditions for online learnability. The rates involve two ingredients: the expressiveness of the policy class under the dynamics, and a stability term measuring how instantaneous loss differs from a counterfactual loss. Matching lower bounds show that both contributions are necessary in the analysis.

The framework recovers regret bounds for online learning with memory, linear quadratic control, online Markov decision processes, and adversarial target tracking. It also gives tight bounds for new problems involving nonlinear dynamics and nonconvex losses. Because the upper bounds are non-constructive, the main contribution is a characterization of achievable learning rates rather than a directly specified general-purpose learning algorithm.
neurips-2020-online-learning-with-dynami.tldr: A minimax analysis characterizes online learning with changing dynamics through policy complexity and dynamical stability.

paragraphs: Large neural recordings capture many neurons across several populations, but interactions between those populations can change over time. This paper models that variation by assigning each population its own low-dimensional latent variables. Those hidden variables evolve dynamically and provide the space through which the populations interact.

A discrete set of dynamical states allows the interaction pattern to switch rather than remain fixed throughout a recording. The transition rules are parameterized to capture which populations are associated with switches between interaction states. The model is fitted using variational expectation-maximization with a structured mean-field approximation, combining inference about latent activity with learning the switching dynamics.

After simulation validation, the authors apply the model to primate motor-area spiking and C. elegans calcium imaging. Both applications reveal behaviorally relevant states with distinct inter-population interactions, along with different populations that predict transitions. The findings provide an interpretable description of changing coordination; predictive associations with switching do not by themselves establish that a population causally triggers a transition.
neurips-2020-recurrent-switching-dynamic.tldr: A switching latent dynamical model identifies changing neural-population interactions and populations that predict transitions between behaviorally relevant states.

paragraphs: A learning agent needs a reason to explore when an environment supplies no external reward. One common curiosity signal measures how poorly a model predicts future observations. The paper points out that this can be problematic when the future is inherently stochastic, because prediction itself may be difficult or ill-posed.

The proposed alternative rewards novel associations between sensory modalities, specifically sight and sound. An audio-visual association model supplies an intrinsic signal based on the relationship between what the agent sees and hears. The approach draws on the role of multiple senses in human exploration and uses their combination to guide the agent's learning.

Experiments in several Atari environments and the photorealistic Habitat navigation simulator show benefits from this association-based curiosity without external rewards. The findings support cross-sensory novelty as a useful source of exploration guidance. The contribution is a different target for curiosity: discovering relationships between sensory inputs, with empirical evidence that this can help agents explore more efficiently.
neurips-2020-see-hear-explore-curiosity-.tldr: Rewarding novel sight–sound associations provides an intrinsic exploration signal that helps agents learn without external rewards.

paragraphs: An empirical average can differ from the underlying expected value. When many functions are considered together, the supremum deviation measures the largest such discrepancy across the family. This paper develops probabilistic bounds on that quantity using empirical centralization, making the guarantees depend on the observed sample.

The bounds have optimal dependence on the largest variance among the functions and on their ranges, while retaining the sample-count dependence of existing bounds. To make the result computable, the authors develop tightly concentrated Monte Carlo estimators of the empirical Rademacher average for the centered family. They also prove concentration results for the empirical maximum variance.

These components connect the theoretical bound to quantities that can be estimated in practice. Experiments show substantially tighter results than non-centralized bounds and practical usefulness even with small samples. The improvement therefore concerns how variance, range, and observed data enter a uniform guarantee, without claiming a better dependence on sample count than the existing bounds used for comparison.
neurips-2020-sharp-uniform-convergence-b.tldr: Empirical centralization yields practical uniform convergence bounds with optimal variance and range dependence and improved empirical tightness.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization uses noisy gradient estimates to improve an objective. Heavy-tailed noise makes reliable guarantees challenging because unusually large gradient errors can matter. This paper studies smooth convex objectives in that setting and introduces clipped-SSTM, a method combining a special accelerated stochastic gradient procedure with gradient clipping.

Clipping limits the magnitude of stochastic gradient updates, while acceleration is built into the underlying optimization method. The authors derive high-probability complexity bounds for clipped-SSTM under heavy-tailed gradient noise. Such bounds describe computational requirements with a probabilistic guarantee, addressing a theoretical gap identified in the abstract.

The method is extended to strongly convex objectives, where the new complexity bounds improve on prior results. The proof technique also yields nontrivial high-probability bounds for ordinary stochastic gradient descent with clipping without assuming light-tailed noise. The contribution is thus both an accelerated algorithm and an analysis applicable to a simpler clipped method, with claims tied to the stated optimization settings.
neurips-2020-stochastic-optimization-wit.tldr: Clipped-SSTM combines acceleration and gradient clipping to obtain high-probability optimization guarantees under heavy-tailed gradient noise.

paragraphs: A variational autoencoder contains a decoder that generates samples and an encoder that infers their latent representations. One might expect the encoder to behave consistently on typical samples from its own decoder. This paper shows that ordinary VAE training does not necessarily provide that property and examines the consequences for learned representations.

The proposed remedy introduces self-consistency through an extended VAE model with a Markov chain alternating between encoder and decoder. An alternative construction of the variational approximation supports training with this requirement. The method can train a model from scratch or serve as a fully self-supervised postprocessing step for an existing VAE without access to its original training data.

Experiments find that encoders trained this way produce representations insensitive to input perturbations introduced by adversarial attacks. Results on ColorMnist and CelebA quantify representation properties and compare against a baseline explicitly trained for the desired property. The findings connect internal encoder–decoder consistency with empirically observed robustness, without asserting that all adversarial perturbations are neutralized.
neurips-2020-the-autoencoding-variationa.tldr: An encoder–decoder self-consistency method improves VAE representations and shows empirical robustness to adversarial input perturbations.

paragraphs: A network trained with stochastic architectures can support different architectures during inference. Research on this capability has often been intertwined with neural architecture search. This paper studies it as a standalone training problem, asking how such networks behave and what inference-time architectural variation can support beyond searching for one architecture.

The investigation examines training stability, convergence, predictive behavior, and generalization to unseen architectures. It identifies problems in the basic approach, including differences between training and testing behavior and function mode collapse. The authors propose remedies informed by theoretical and empirical analysis, using those findings to improve the stochastic-architecture model.

The improved approach is applied to model ensembles, uncertainty estimation, and semi-supervised learning. Reported CIFAR-10 results include a 2.75% error rate and an expected calibration error of 0.0032. These outcomes support the effectiveness of the evaluated model across the explored uses. The broader contribution is treating architectural stochasticity as a useful modeling capability with its own training challenges and applications.
neurips-2020-understanding-and-exploring.tldr: The paper studies and improves stochastic-architecture training for ensembles, uncertainty estimation, and semi-supervised learning beyond architecture search.
